entry.title: Two months across America, planned with AI
entry.content:
Five anchors, every booking, the price drops and an 80-page book.

This summer we took a two-month family trip across the US, built around the World Cup. AI handled most of the planning, and I have to say it was an amazing experience. If I’d had to plan it myself, I wouldn’t even know where to start.

It also went far beyond suggesting a few places to visit. Here’s what it actually did.

It built the route

I didn’t hand it an itinerary to polish. I gave it five fixed points:

  1. Start in New York (to visit family, and the flights are more convenient).
  2. Be at 2-3 World Cup matches in the early, not-expensive stages.
  3. Orlando (parks).
  4. Miami (for a cruise).
  5. St. Louis (to visit family).

That’s it. From there it started asking questions, making suggestions and building a route.

The best example is Hershey, Pennsylvania, a place I’d never have thought of going through. Lucky the AI suggested it: a town built entirely around the chocolate factory, with an amusement park and a huge water park, in an area surrounded by Amish communities.

It planned the days

Once we had a route, it suggested a plan for each day and where to stay.

It made the bookings

Every hotel, every flight and every restaurant was handled and booked by AI.

That includes the small questions you’d normally leave for later. It wrote to a restaurant in Brooklyn to ask if we could also reserve the bar upstairs after dinner (no, but there’s a waiting list you join when you arrive), and what “open until 10pm” really meant (10pm is the last reservation, and they stay open until the last party finishes).

It handled the boring parts

This is the part I’d have hated most. AI helped me with the car rental, the insurance, the tolls and fees and everything around them.

It kept hunting for better prices

Booking wasn’t the end of it. AI kept monitoring prices, and when one dropped, it got me a better deal.

Here’s one real example, five nights at a hotel in Brooklyn, with the same room type and the same dates:

When Where Total
May 14 First booking $1,536.79
May 25 Rebooked after a drop $1,509.25
June 3 Moved to another booking site $1,408.28

That’s $128.51 off one stay, without me having to check anything. On June 3 the old booking was cancelled for free and the new one was confirmed a minute apart.

It helped with the hard parts too

The parks. Orlando was going to cost a lot of money and time, and I had no energy for planning it. So that’s how Park Autopilot started.

The World Cup. AI also helped me get tickets from FIFA, which turned into its own story.

It stayed with us on the road

The help didn’t end when we left. As a rule, every route also came with a story from ChatGPT. In St. Louis, a city I’d never heard of (I couldn’t even have pointed to Missouri on a map), we spent a few days touring and learning the history and culture with the chat.

It created the book

AI created a whole 80-page book covering the entire route: what to do, anecdotes and so on. And we printed it.

If you’re considering something similar, feel free to ask.

entry.title: I accidentally tracked the World Cup ticket market
entry.content:
I just wanted two tickets for my son. Like every side project, it got out of control.

A year ago we decided to take the kids to the World Cup. I thought the hard part would be flights and hotels. Wrong. What started as an attempt to get a few tickets for the family turned into a super fun, super nerdy project.

If you haven’t been through this, you’d assume you just go to the site and buy a ticket. That’s not how it works. FIFA sells tickets through lotteries, different sales rounds and an official secondary market. In some cases you don’t even know who’s playing in the match you’re buying.

We, for example, bought a ticket to a match. There was a date, a stadium and a time. There were no teams. Months later came the draw and we got Germany against Ecuador. We paid for a match without having any idea who’d play in it. Luckily we ended up with good ones. It was worth a lot of money, but very risky.

Meanwhile a huge community of Israelis formed around getting tickets (respect to @FarageMoshe!). People bought for each other, held tickets for each other and helped each other understand the system. And every FIFA drop landed at the worst possible moment: holiday dinners, meetings, Friday dinners and the middle of the night.

You also have to understand that FIFA doesn’t only sell the tickets. It also operates the secondary market. So it earns when a ticket is first sold, and again when it’s resold. The total commission reaches almost 30% of the transaction. Across hundreds of thousands of tickets, that’s a huge money machine.

Then it got out of control

My son is an England fanatic and was gutted we didn’t get them, so we really tried to get an England ticket. I noticed I was opening FIFA’s site about 30 times a day, which didn’t help, because FIFA’s site is terrible. At some point I realized I needed automation.

So I built a small system with Claude. At first it was supposed to do one thing: show me the cheapest price for a pair of tickets. Then I added price tracking. Then inventory tracking. Then history. Then graphs. Then more graphs. Like every side project, it got out of control.

Without meaning to, the system started collecting a daily snapshot of almost the entire World Cup ticket market. How many tickets are available, what they cost, how prices change, which matches are heating up and which are cooling down. Suddenly I wasn’t looking at single matches anymore, but at the whole market.

I started posting some of the insights on Reddit. I thought maybe a few dozen people would read them. In practice they turned into discussions with hundreds of comments, people from all over the world started sending me stories and data, and at some point I even found myself talking to journalists trying to understand what was happening to ticket prices.

And in the end I did manage to catch two tickets to the round of 32 in Atlanta (assuming England gets there) at a relatively reasonable price. We can’t actually get to Atlanta in the end, but never mind. Goal achieved. And sitting on mountains of data gave me a view that only FIFA has, and doesn’t publish.

What the data shows

These are the prices as of June 11, 2026.

There are no cheap matches. Austria against Jordan starts at around $115, Jordan against Algeria at around $119, and Cape Verde against Saudi Arabia at around $138. And those are just the cheapest tickets. Want a reasonable seat, or to sit together? Now you’re talking about $300-400.

Big matches aren’t just a bit more expensive.

Match Cheapest Median
Germany vs Curaçao ~$345 ~$743
France vs Senegal $539 $1,144
Argentina vs Algeria $619 $1,173
Netherlands vs Japan $656 $1,178
England vs Croatia $747 $1,460
Scotland vs Brazil (Miami) ~$1,610 ~$2,760
Colombia vs Portugal ~$2,530 ~$4,600

All of that is for group stage games. We haven’t even reached the decisive rounds.

And the final? The cheapest ticket currently stands at around $9,085. The median is getting close to $20,000. Yes, for one football match.

The funniest part was seeing what people try to sell. I saw a ticket to Netherlands against Sweden at $10.9 million, Paraguay against Australia at $5.1 million, round of 16 tickets at almost $8 million, and a ticket to the final at $11.5 million.

And the best story? Haiti against Scotland. I’d have sworn it would be a $100 match when I saw the draw. It turns out Scottish fans, who waited decades for a World Cup, organized like an invasion force. They took over a town near Boston, rented a fleet of buses, and private groups popped up just to connect buyers and sellers and get around FIFA’s commission.

On top of that, Boston has a large Haitian community that went just as crazy. And suddenly you can see it in the numbers: inventory cut from around 2,100 tickets to fewer than 700. Today the cheapest entry costs around $552, and a regular seat around $850.

The system is still running and collecting data, and I think it’s about to get even more interesting. A lot of people waited for the last minute because they were sure prices would drop. So far that isn’t happening. On the contrary, lately it sometimes takes half an hour just to get into the marketplace.

Let’s hope the tournament justifies it!

entry.title: Why I gave my agents a company
entry.content:
We already know how to build products in teams. Let’s not reinvent the wheel.

I know it’s a cliché, but this has been one of the most fun and productive periods I can remember. The number of projects, tools and products I’m building makes no sense, and the ability to get from an idea to something working blows my mind every time.

But beyond that, it keeps making me think about the future development model. Two things in particular occupy me.

The interface. Claude Code brought a revolution in how we work. It was an experiment that opened a lot of doors and took the development world (and not only it) by storm. But as I move forward and build bigger things, I feel how limited and uncomfortable this interface is. There’s a reason we once moved from working in the CLI to IDEs.

The velocity gap. There were always differences in speed between a small startup and a big company. A bug in some small project is not a bug in Gmail, that’s clear. But today’s velocity gap between AI-first companies (which are naturally smaller and younger) and mature companies is impossible to ignore, and there’s a reason the latter are stressed.

So with every new project that’s big enough, I try to challenge my way of working. There’s something new every week, and I want to grow not only in the projects I do, but in how I do them. I already shared one iteration, and I recently upgraded it.

Copy what already works

In the end I’m a big believer in not reinventing the wheel. Building a product isn’t new. There’s a lot of organizational knowledge and working methods out there: building expertise, teamwork, dividing work, efficient communication, handoffs, task management, orderly review, direction from above. I think we should use them.

What does that mean? A team needs a mix of people who each understand something specific. People can do several things, but someone has to be responsible. You need an organized board, so the project manager can see failures and the manager can see what’s stuck. You need a company chat where anyone can ask questions and see what happened.

My idea is to copy the functioning companies and teams I’ve worked in, and bring that into the world of agents.

What I built

I call it MissionControl (the screenshot above shows it under the name AgentBoard). It has six parts.

A team. Different personas, but also different tools. The developers are Claude Code processes (one shot). QA uses Google’s local models, because QA burns through tokens. Marketing is OpenAI connected to a Chrome MCP. Each one is built differently, with its own direction and tools.

A board. Mostly visibility for me into what’s happening, where and how. It also lets the project manager throttle the work (only two tickets running at a time), and shows me what’s waiting for me and what needs review. And every finished task goes to the project manager, who decides whether follow-up tasks need to go into the backlog.

A company chat. Like Slack. Anyone can give an opinion, ask questions and suggest things, bots and people alike. You can see what happened overnight and even mention specific bots (or people). There are rooms by topic and all of that.

Logs. What happened in this task, why we got here, how we reached one decision or another and how long it took. Every bot keeps a log of its run that you can dive into the moment something goes wrong.

Review. Some things need approval: because they aren’t trivial, because we want to make sure we’re aligned, or because a decision is going to cost money. For that, bots need sign-off. Right now only I approve, but other bots could too (think of a CFO with a limited budget).

A timeline. A high-level view of what happened recently, which gives a good snapshot of what we’re focused on and how long things take.

All of this together is my home page for the project. I sample it a few times a day, and usually when I wake up in the morning there are quite a few tasks waiting for me.

Why it matters

First, I think this will enable a lot of things that got stuck in the CLI, and help people who struggle with it. I don’t think a CLI is the most comfortable place to understand what’s going on, and the smarter agents get, the wider the picture you want.

Second, it’s closer to what organizations are used to, so it should be easier to digest. That goes both for connecting to existing systems and for connecting to existing processes.

Third, it lets you split the work more comfortably into small, efficient pieces. Claude Code isn’t good at everything. Local models are much cheaper. Some things need a big context, and for others context only gets in the way. And no less important, we have to free ourselves from our own computers. Things have to start running independently somewhere remote, without us keeping our laptops awake all the time.

To be clear, this is me playing around with personal projects. It’s not production-ready in any way. I build it over weekends, purely to learn how far I can get. What gave me the push was Google’s latest models, which can work locally at a reasonable (relatively) level, so I can do this without burning a lot of money.

entry.title: Building it was the easy part
entry.content:
To bring in a dollar for every fifty cents you spend, you first have to spend thousands without seeing a cent.

So you fell for the LinkedIn drugs. You decided to show Avishai the senior engineer that you can work with AI too. Now you’re going to have your own fitness app, you’re going to make millions on it, and who does he think he is anyway.

A month later, after regretting seven times that you ever opened LinkedIn when you could have been watching recipes on Instagram, you actually managed to make your virtual coach give decent advice, other than eating a kilo and a half of chicken breast at 11pm.

But now what?

This is the part I always got stuck on. As a technical person I had piles of projects that reached the finish line only to stay there. Wonderful products with one user (me). That’s the dream and the heartbreak of many people I’ve talked to lately, who realized that building is only the first piece of the puzzle.

After I finished the Disney project I thought the army of bots I’d built might be able to help with this too. In the same way we built the product, I asked the CEO to start bringing in some business, because the investors aren’t happy. And to do it as cheaply as possible, because the investors have a trip to the US this summer and there isn’t much money left.

After the usual things (mostly SEO), this is what we tried:

  • A rich blog about Disney and people’s pain points. It built itself a schedule of posts, like an entire marketing team, based mostly on what people search for.
  • A free countdown. It spotted a pattern of people posting when they’re about to travel, so it built a nice, free countdown for them to share.
  • A referral campaign. It mapped influencers and sites, opened a referral campaign with a discount, created a coupon code for each one and sent personal emails.
  • Instagram outreach. It found Instagram influencers who are relatively reachable there and started sending them personal messages.

All of it automated. The ideas were all its own, after my approval. Most of them yield nothing, of course, but marketing is about big numbers and time.

And to be clear, I also had one Claude session reaching out to people on Instagram while another went through user feedback and fixed things. Don’t do this. They’ll probably block your account at some point.

In the end this isn’t magic. It’s very, very hard to bring in users and rise above the noise. There are no big shortcuts here, and if you don’t have the financial backing to pour piles of money into ads, you’ll have to work hard, for a long time.

Update: the final tally was about $1,000 in total. Reddit banned me, 60 Disney bloggers brought 0 paying users, and we ended up with 45+ SEO posts and even taxi tablets in Orlando. The building took about 10 hours. The distribution was the real experiment.

entry.title: I gave my side project a CEO
entry.content:
From a messy idea to a live product in a week, for about 10 hours of my time.

A couple of weeks ago I had an idea, thanks to the endless digging I was doing for our family trip to the US. I realized I was about to pour a lot of money and time into our days in Orlando, and I really had no energy for it. So on Sunday morning I threw a few disorganized lines into ChatGPT’s research mode.

Once we understood there might be something interesting here, I asked it for a detailed product spec. The plan was to hand that to Claude Code. But first, I put together a team.

Hiring the team

I created a sub-agent for every function in the organization. I made some of them with Claude and took others from this list.

If you haven’t used them, a sub-agent in Claude is an agent with its own context and abilities that doesn’t pollute the global context too much. More importantly, it can work in the background, so a single task can have the server code and the frontend code written in parallel.

Then I gave the CEO the 15-page research PDF from ChatGPT and the product spec, and asked for a roadmap with everything we’d need.

My conversation with the CEO focused on what I wanted to achieve: a small project that tests whether there’s a business here and doesn’t cost me money.

Very quickly the CEO produced a task board split into phases. Two things are important to understand here:

  1. My only interface was the Claude Code CLI. I had no idea (and didn’t care) what files it was creating or what the code looked like.
  2. The code was only a small part of the work. There were a lot of tasks around the written content, the design language and how to market the thing.

Letting them run

From there it was just running. There are tasks, get to work.

It was still slow, though. It worked on one task at a time, even when it split that task between sub-agents. So I simply opened about five Claude Codes running in parallel and tried to keep them from stepping on each other. If they did, I didn’t care. Let them figure it out.

What mattered most to me was not having to deal with it, because I have things to do. So I told them every task had to go through deep validation, and I wanted them to run for as long as possible while I was away from the computer. Some Claude Code sessions ran across several tasks for a few hours.

Management problems

Pretty soon I had no idea what was going on. I just wanted to know where we stood. Had we shipped already and were we making millions, or were we still in design?

The tasks lived in a markdown file the CEO had created and kept updating, so I asked for a visualization on top of it. That’s how a simple JS dashboard was born.

This is where it got a bit complicated, because everyone updated the file differently and kept breaking the dashboard. So I asked the project manager to take ownership: everything goes through them, they keep the file to a schema, and it stops breaking every other day. I even threatened to fire them.

What it’s like to be a product manager

Back to the project itself. I started from a problem I actually had, and it was a pleasure not to be bothered with the tactical level. Is there an API for this? Will it take forever? How do we pull it? How do we show it in real time?

I didn’t go into any of that. Let it break its own head on those. I suddenly understood how much fun it is to be a product manager.

Behind the scenes it really did find and solve all of those problems. Then it had to be released, which is usually where I’d step in and help with the setup. But again, I had no energy or desire for that.

So I let go completely. I told it which services I already pay for, and to find the rest by itself. It made all the decisions about services on its own (think how much money there is in that market). It opened accounts for what it needed, I connected a Cloudflare MCP, gave it the API keys it asked for, and it wired and configured everything.

This would be very scary in a company’s production environment, but I’m on a side project, working with:

claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --chrome

Getting traffic

It told me which domain to buy, and we had a site. Now we needed traffic, so it mapped out what to do:

  1. It suggested what to write on Reddit. Reddit blocks bots, and very quickly it blocked me too.
  2. It wrote an entire blog for SEO, images included.
  3. Growth hacking with Claude in Chrome.

It even mapped influencers, created a coupon code for each one and wrote them a personal email based on the content they publish. Across the whole site, on the home page and in every touchpoint outside it, it decided on the angle and the content. I only told it the goal.

The nice part is that during the build I got two really big pieces of feedback from friends:

  1. Make the site super specific to one park instead of something generic.
  2. Make the experience experiential rather than analytical, with a story and effects.

I copied the feedback as is and started discussing it with the CEO. These were big changes, and it broke them down.

The bottom line

From idea to production, everything included, in a week. My own net time on it was maybe 10 hours, here and there.

From what I peeked at, this is a technologically complicated project. It would probably have taken me a few months to build by myself, which is crazy.

If you want to try it or have feedback, it’s at parkautopilot.com.

entry.title: It doesn't matter
entry.content:
Pick something and start building. The FOMO isn’t real.

It doesn’t matter which model you use. The differences aren’t that big.

It doesn’t matter which tool you built the site with. Everyone copies everyone anyway, and your users have no idea.

It doesn’t matter that they released something new yesterday. You don’t have to try it right away.

It doesn’t matter that there’s another product and another announcement and another way of doing things. So what. The world doesn’t flip overnight because that guy said so.

It doesn’t matter that the guy on LinkedIn said something is dead. He’s an influencer in his own eyes, with 92 followers.

It doesn’t matter that there’s a new feature you “must use”, or that there’s a prompt enhancer and a prompt enrichment and a prompt compressor. It all amounts to nothing. I promise you that even the people saying it changed their world don’t feel the difference.

It doesn’t matter, all the people who talk and write posts and send links and speak at conferences and get interviewed on podcasts and run newsletters and announce that last night, while everyone was asleep, there was an earthquake and only they felt it.

What matters is doing. Building, experimenting, feeling it with your own hands.

I’ll always prefer someone who built an app all the way through, in whatever IDE, over someone with 18 open tabs of unfinished projects.

In job interviews, a working product will beat any blog post. In the long run, the ones who do win, and the ones who only talk get found out.

Don’t forget what matters. Don’t get blinded by words and talk, and remember what the goal is. So just pick something and start building. Let go of the FOMO, it doesn’t exist.

entry.title: AI shines in the 20% you hate
entry.content:
Take your thing all the way, put it out in the world, and only then form an opinion.

This was my first real vibe coding project.

I’ve already said I play with AI a lot in the free time I don’t have. But there’s a huge difference between playing by yourself and putting something out there, with users and everything. So I really insisted with myself on going beyond the fast 80% and finishing the job, including the remaining, exhausting 20%.

For me personally, that’s the biggest impact AI has on indie developers. The 80% was always easy for me. My problem was always the worlds of design, marketing, writing the copy and so on. I have no doubt it isn’t going to replace those professionals, but it really does close that gap and give you “good enough” results. (Which is why I’d be quite worried if I were a mediocre professional.)

The project, briefly

Briefly, because it’s not the point of this post. Over the past year I started training intensely, and after a visit to the doctor I understood I also had to change my diet to match. As someone who had never tracked his weight or what he puts in his mouth, I suddenly needed to know how much protein was in every meal. I needed a “personal assistant” that knows me and is always available, say through WhatsApp.

Letting go of the reins

Something I tried to emphasize was using AI tools as much as possible, even for the architecture and which frameworks to use. I obviously have opinions there, but I wanted to open my mind and let go of the reins specifically in the places I know, as practice. It paid off at the end of the project, when ChatGPT answered, in my place, the entire email exchange with Paddle about their many questions and comments.

And AI didn’t only save me time (or money). In this project I saw how it gives me things I simply wouldn’t have thought of. The initial goal was to give myself an easy personal assistant for my training, conveniently through WhatsApp. In our first (uncompromising) brainstorm it had a lot of comments, and thanks to it we arrived at many more bots that could be useful. It built the entire catalog, the images and everything around it, which I’d never have gotten to.

Finish it

I think that’s exactly where AI shines: in the 20% you hate, or wouldn’t bother with. So I really push everyone playing with this: if you want to see the biggest added value, take your thing all the way, put it out in the world, and don’t form an opinion until you’ve done that.

The project is at helps-hub.com.

Update: the honest outcome is few users. The lesson was that I built the whole thing before anyone asked for it. Getting people to care is its own project.

entry.title: AI is coming for the rubber ducks
entry.content:
My copilot went from code monkey to the one I think out loud with.

In software development there’s a concept called rubber ducking. It’s when, while trying to find out what went wrong in your code, you talk to someone imaginary and explain what you’re doing. The really devout put an actual rubber duck next to their desk and start talking to it (hence the name).

Besides reinforcing the stigma about how weird programmers are, it’s a process that’s generally been shown to help with solving problems. Sometimes in your head you skip things “because they’re trivial”, and just saying them out loud is enough to see what the problem is.

Why am I telling you this? Because lately I’ve picked up a habit of “talking” to Copilot, or to whatever AI tool I’m working with at the moment. During development I keep writing to it what I want to do now, why I’m doing it and how I think it should be implemented.

A lot of the time it’s just there with me, saying “sounds good bro, go for it”. But it also often asks me more questions along the way, offers another angle, or puts the information aside and brings it up later.

That’s very different from how I used it at first, when it was simply my executor: I told it what to do, down to which function and how. Slowly its role is becoming less code monkey and more of a partner through the whole process.

It’s also a good habit. It helps me not miss things, and on the other side it gives the tool more context and therefore better results. (Although sometimes that context isn’t relevant, like when and where I’m going to give the talk we’re working on slides for. But why not.)

In short, the first industry AI is going to kill is rubber ducks.

entry.title: Employer branding can't be faked
entry.content:
Ten things that worked for me, and why a thousand campaigns won’t save a bad place to work.

What is employer branding, anyway?

If branding is what people think about what your company does or builds, employer branding is what current and potential employees think about the company. The two aren’t orthogonal, but they also aren’t as directly connected as people think.

For example, I think a Tesla is a great car, but I’m not sure I’d want a boss like Musk. The best example I always give is Pornhub: a company many people would hesitate to attach their name to, whose engineering brand is actually very good.

And why do you need it? Almost always for hiring and retention. When hiring gets hard, everyone remembers employer branding, although the conversation often turns shallow (who’s performing at the Purim party, for example). It doesn’t have to be that way.

Over the last few years a number of people consulted with me about this, partly because WeWork managed to build a good employer brand in Israel (amazing work by Ron Gura, whom I learned a lot from). Here’s some of what worked for me:

1. Retention comes before hiring. Many people think employer branding should focus on recruiting, but retention is more important. What good is filling a leaking bucket? If you focus only on recruiting, the people already in the organization feel less important. That’s what you’re spending money on? Why didn’t you invest like this in me?

2. Don’t build an image for nothing. A big company can’t move fast, so there’s no point pumping that message (“we operate like a startup without the financial pressure of a startup!”) only for people to arrive, see it isn’t so, and leave after six months. Understand your real relative strengths, and double down on them.

3. Empower people. That’s how you create a culture of people who are proud of where they work. A CEO speaking at a conference is a drop in the ocean. Dozens of employees who keep writing about how interesting and fun their work is, that’s an army. And invest in people in general. It seems like good advice regardless, even if they never write a post about you.

4. Think hard about the DNA you want to create, and act on it. We had a good candidate who we asked, during her interviews, why she wanted to join us. She said she missed the feeling she’d had at another startup, where they worked into the evening and then all went out together. I told her it would be a shame for her to come, because it wouldn’t be like that with us.

5. Remember the candidates you reject. Your image forms in everyone who has interacted with the company. Do you know the biggest group that interacts with you, and that you ignore? Candidates, specifically the ones who didn’t get in (probably 90% of the pipeline). They’ll end up at another company, and your name might come up. Candidates with a bad experience will make sure to tell everyone how much you suck.

6. It’s never too early. You probably need to think about this from day one. It’s a long process, and the first people who join teach a lot about the company you’re building and shape the culture and what you stand for. Employer branding is more and more activities whose fruits you sometimes see only after months or years.

7. Can’t talk about what you do? Focus on the goal. Focus on the mission rather than the specific solution. Our product changed a lot, but our goal, helping developers grow professionally in a playful way, stayed relatively stable.

8. People. People. People. People want to work with good people, who are fun to be around and who they can learn from. Few people are interested in insurance, but Lemonade has amazing people. What you do is nice, but for many people it isn’t the most critical thing, and who their manager is matters more. Invest in bringing in good people, from the start.

9. Share. You’re not working on the atomic bomb here. Nothing will happen if everyone sees how you’re progressing. Share failures too, because no company is all roses. The more information people have, the shorter the due diligence in interviews, and the fewer false positives.

10. More than anything, you can’t fake it. If the company isn’t a good place to work, a thousand campaigns won’t fix that. If there are toxic people, they’ll poison everyone who comes. And if there are no big, interesting problems, maybe you don’t need hundreds of people who are all seniors.

entry.title: Five startups for Apple's beauty score
entry.content:
Investors, my DMs are open.

This week Apple launched a lot of new things. It’s very easy to latch on to the AI announcements, but at the bottom of the list they managed to develop a groundbreaking algorithm: take a picture and give it a score for how beautiful it is.

It turns out they lied to us our whole lives about beauty being in the eye of the beholder. Now it can be scientifically proven that the painting hanging in your pretentious art-loving friend’s living room is absolutely ugly.

So in honor of the new API, I thought of a few products that could be built around it:

1. A camera app for men that won’t let you exit until the photo is above a certain threshold. It solves the problem where they ask you to take a picture and then it’s “wait wait, again, I didn’t come out nice”. From now on you can say “babe, I gave you two 82s and an 89, leave me alone”.

2. An app that automatically detects fake compliments on photos of the nephews in the family group and responds: “Yahli can’t possibly be gorgeous, this picture is a 40 at most”.

3. An app that detects too big a gap between the original photo and the one you’re trying to upload to Instagram, and warns you that you overdid the filters: “According to the app you’re trying to upload a 90, even though according to face recognition you’re a 65 on a good day, please remove”.

4. An app that helps you choose the best Tinder photo. It could really help with men who upload a picture with a headset and a microphone.

5. An app that connects to the work WhatsApp group, and every time someone posts a baby photo, gives you the appropriate politically correct response: “The system detected a baby with a score of 17, which corresponds to ‘very clearly a baby, mazel tov’”. You could easily upsell through a partnership with the app from item 2.

entry.title: There is no recipe
entry.content:
I replaced all the exclamation marks at the end of my sentences with question marks.

A lot of people ask me why I don’t share about Wilco anymore, and it’s a question I find a bit hard to answer.

There are the obvious reasons, which I learned the hard way:

  1. The bigger a company gets, the slower things move, so not much changes.
  2. We’re not alone anymore. There’s a team, investors and customers, so you have to censor yourself more.
  3. When there are fewer successes, there’s less to share.

But I want to write about the fourth reason.

The programmer’s way

The hardest part for me, as a programmer entering the world of entrepreneurship, was that there was no “recipe” I could follow.

As a programmer, when I hit a problem I go do research. I read books, talk to my network, learn from past cases. After collecting data you quickly start seeing patterns. The solution space turns out to be pretty closed, and you understand the pros and cons of each alternative.

That’s how I thought it would be when we started thinking about raising money. We weren’t sure at all when the right time was, or how much. So I started asking a lot of entrepreneurs who’d been there, experienced people I hold in high regard, some of whom had built big companies.

To my surprise, I simply got a huge and contradictory amount of opinions:

  • Stay at your job as long as possible so you can work with a clear head. Leave as soon as possible, because it looks bad to investors and you have to give 200%.
  • Take a few months to work on a product and then raise. Don’t build anything, it’s easier to raise on just an idea.
  • Raise the bare minimum so you come into the next round strong. Don’t you dare raise small, funds love a clean cap table.
  • Hire an advisor to take care of it. Don’t you dare bring in someone who’ll take a percentage.
  • Bring as many customers as you can, even for free. Free customers aren’t interesting, one paying customer beats ten free ones.
  • Emphasize the solution. The solution doesn’t matter, emphasize the problem. Emphasize the team, everything’s going to change later anyway.
  • Don’t talk to funds at all. Don’t talk to angels at all. Start spreading the word.

The peak was when a very close mentor warmly suggested we close a customer from abroad, to show how strong we are for bringing in a customer from outside our network. We managed to close one. A few weeks later we presented to one of the strongest people in Israeli high tech, and he simply scolded us for looking for customers abroad, because it actually showed how weak our network was.

I walked out of that conversation in shock. Then I remembered a tip I got from Ron Gura and Nimrod Priell, on two separate occasions: you can read and learn until tomorrow, but in entrepreneurship you just have to try and develop instincts. It’s a muscle you have to train.

So we started letting go, trusting ourselves more, and gave ourselves permission to be wrong.

I was an idiot

When I started this journey two years ago (it feels like a decade), I had a very well-formed idea of how a startup should be run. I’d read all the books and listened to all the podcasts. I’d even been in a company or two from the very beginning. I thought I was coming with a recipe and just had to execute it.

I was an idiot.

I don’t think there’s a single thing I once believed to be true about entrepreneurship that I haven’t changed my mind about. The path to growth, how to build a team, what to do to bring in customers, how to build the product. If there’s one thing I’ve learned, mostly in the last year, it’s that I don’t know anything. A great lesson in humility, delivered by a flying kick.

Since then I walk around the world not believing anything professional, from anyone. If someone speaks with confidence, I scorn them. My whole foundation was shaken. As far as I’m concerned, every piece of advice I read was written by ChatGPT with a hallucination.

Obviously that’s an exaggeration too, but I sit at meetups where founders recite mantras and I want to stand up and say, “Glad it worked for you in 2017. I tried what you said, I suggest nobody does it, it doesn’t work, gentlemen.”

I was so captive to the concept that I convinced myself there was a direct link between what we did and the outcome, when in practice things bigger than us plus luck played a much bigger role. As a deterministic person, that’s discouraging. It’s like looking at an A/B test with two opposite results. It makes you lose faith in the method.

Back to natural size

So this past year has mostly made me lower my voice. I don’t have the privilege of speaking unequivocally. I replaced all the exclamation marks at the end of my sentences with question marks. When people come to me for advice I hedge, and when an issue comes up I analyze it, but I always understand that a lot of it doesn’t depend on what I do.

At the end of the day it brings you down to your natural size, and it makes me, at least, focus on just doing. And then doing more and more and more, until at some point something hits, and I won’t know why. So I’ll just keep going, and focus more on doing and less on talking.

entry.title: The mysterious journey of becoming a senior engineer
entry.content:
What got you here won’t get you there.

This is the written version of my talk at Reversim, for anyone who missed it.

I’ve worked in individual contributor roles at WeWork, Facebook and now Wilco: Senior, Staff and CTO (which I also consider more of an IC role).

The story starts when I joined WeWork. In my first team meeting they introduced me and another developer as the seniors of the group. Coming from startups, I thought everyone was senior. I didn’t understand that we were the seniors. So I had no choice but to go and research it, and I wrote a bit about what I learned.

I’ve learned a lot since then, mainly how to manage yourself day to day. And I realized there are many confused people like me, so we need to start talking about role definitions and expectations more concretely.

The problem

Most developers’ paths look similar. You start by learning what programming even means, and everything is new. Slowly you become more and more independent and get more responsibility. You progress from junior to mid-level, and one day you become the team’s knowledge hub, the one who knows all the hidden corners of the code.

And then what?

Until now everything went (relatively) smoothly. You got a task and finished it, got a bigger task and finished that too. Now you want to know what the next step is. You look up and see two options: management or architecture.

Why bother? As an individual, you want more impact and more independence, and advancement often translates into more money. As an organization, you want people to progress because it helps you build strength and helps you retain people.

Sounds good, so what’s the problem?

There’s a pretty clear, linear, standard path at the start. But when you reach the “senior” worlds, it gets messy: too many titles that say the same thing and at the same time say nothing, and no clarity about what’s expected of you or what the difference is between them.

Management is a little clearer. That path has existed longer, it exists in other professions, and enough has been said about it. The senior jump is fairly new, and not that intuitive.

There’s also a problem between the individual and the company. As an individual I depend heavily on my manager to guide me, because the role definitions don’t make it clear what I’m supposed to do. I’m supposed to prove myself through technical projects, and those aren’t always on the table, or at least I don’t know about them.

It’s hard from the manager’s side too. Middle managers are the busiest layer in the organization, because they have to handle the high level and also be there for the small details. And they don’t have many chances to let people practice safely, because failures have a real cost.

Change how you think

The first and most important thing is changing your mindset. For the first time on this career graph, what got you here won’t get you there.

Until now you were used to receiving problems or tasks and solving them. First a small bug, later a huge feature. Now it’s different: you have to go looking for problems.

You’ll also constantly wear different hats, sometimes several at once:

  1. Technical, rolling up your sleeves and working in the code.
  2. Product, understanding the code and knowing how to steer the product.
  3. Project manager, knowing the system and able to steer long processes.

And above all of them: communication and working with people.

The flywheel

Once you know how to think, you need a framework to start spinning a flywheel:

  1. Look for problems.
  2. Build, because that’s why we’re here in the end.
  3. Transfer knowledge, a step where many people fall, creating quite a bit of antagonism.

Looking for a problem is the first and most important stage. It can take a while, and the key is to understand what scope you’re aiming for, so aligning with your manager is very important. You don’t want something too small in time or too big for what you can do.

Define the end goal. Too many times people set off without a concrete definition of what winning looks like. The last thing you want at the end of a project is a conversation about whether you reached the goal. You need to know that beforehand.

Concrete is exactly what most role definitions aren’t. Here are a few real examples, and how to turn them from amorphous into something you can aim at:

The role definition says Make it
Improves code structure and architecture in service of testability and maintainability Decrease the number of bugs in this area of the product by x%
Participates in the hiring process (by submitting referrals, meeting candidates, attending recruiting events) Improve the hiring pipeline by x%
Ensures that knowledge is shared amongst the team and does not position themselves or others as a single point of failure Open source the tool the team built and deliver a recurring workshop to the rest of the company

Don’t leave things in the air. Aim at specific numbers, so you know when it’s good enough and you can move on.

Prepare. You have a project and you know what needs doing, but often you can’t start right away. You’re missing technical knowledge, familiarity with the relevant code, the people involved. Take time to prepare, especially on projects that will take weeks.

Match the scope to the level. The same problem can be solved in several circles and on several timescales. The more senior you are, the more comprehensive the solution you’ll be asked for. The emphasis isn’t necessarily on time (although they usually correlate), but on how much of the problem the solution covers.

Then do it again. The hard part is that you have to repeat this process again and again. One project like this usually isn’t enough. You need to show you can deliver over and over. So create a kind of ritual that keeps the flywheel turning. And remember that the searching stage can be long and shouldn’t take 100% of your time, so you’ll usually have a few balls in the air, each at a different stage.

You own it

You may be at a great organization that takes care of its employees, and I really hope you have a wonderful manager who’s always on top of this. Even so, you’re the one who has to manage your professional development and your promotion.

Things change, managers move, projects get canceled. Don’t leave this journey to fate.

To sum it up:

  • Always be the one who initiates. You can’t wait for opportunities to come to you.
  • Build a plan. Understand where you stand and what you have left.
  • Stay on top of it, track it, and show others you’re meeting your goals.

entry.title: Startups don't have to burn you out
entry.content:
If you work like a crazy person, eventually you go crazy.

In the last few weeks I had several conversations with people I’d be happy to have working with me. They said they’re afraid to make the move, mainly because of what it would do to their work-life balance. So here’s how we see it, and why I think it doesn’t have to be that way.

How I burned out

Let’s start many years ago. Around 2012 I joined a startup as the first employee, in my twenties and with no kids. I basically had nothing much to do in life other than go to a Maccabi game once a week. The two founders had already been working for about half a year without salaries, and I joined right after the fundraise.

It was a great time. I learned a ton and grew professionally in an exceptional way. On the other hand, work was my life. I worked something like 12 hours a day and didn’t have much room for anything else.

It’s important to say that nobody told me to stay, and nobody made a face when I left at 5 (for a Maccabi game). It just worked that way, by inertia.

This also wasn’t a two-week crunch before a release, or a month for some event. We ran like that for more than three years. I didn’t feel it was bad (I’m learning and growing!), and nobody was there to tell me to stop. Even when my eldest daughter was born it didn’t change. A few days at home and, hop, back to it.

Half a year later everything started to collapse. A chain of unrelated events, a family crisis, health problems with my daughter and a deal that fell through, all drained together, and I simply crashed.

I couldn’t get out of bed. I spent whole months either at playgrounds or in hospitals. In hindsight I understood it was burnout. In real time it was just 0% energy.

It was a formative event for me. Since then I’ve been very careful about a few rules to protect this, and more than that, it’s important for me to pass it on to the people working with me and to create a balanced work environment.

Because that’s the thing about work-life balance: it’s like sand, and it will easily slip through your fingers if you don’t pay attention.

What I do now

Since then I make sure to have at least one short day, and the vast majority of the time I close the computer at 6pm. Even in more stressful periods. Even when I was in leadership positions.

I can do that because the group plans ahead, understands that resources are limited, and tries to get the most out of them assuming people work 8 hours a day (or even less).

There’s a lot to say about how you do each thing: good communication, pedantic planning, the ability to adjust while moving, people raising flags often. But it starts with the basic constraint. We have X person-hours, and that won’t move, no matter what. You can’t play with those numbers. Now let’s see what we can do, and when.

That conversation is what we started from as founders. The three of us left very comfortable (and well-paid) jobs, we all have kids, we all have hobbies, and we knew we weren’t going to hurt that. We say it out loud to investors too: we’re going to kill ourselves for this every day, and then we’re going to go help with bath time.

How it usually happens

What usually happens in startups looks like this. The founders, who are very invested, work very hard. The beginning of a company is chaotic and there’s always something to do. More people join and carry on the same way, by inertia.

Then the first version comes out, not exactly on time of course (that’s software projects for you), and everyone works very hard on it, and that’s how the snowball grows. More employees join an existing reality, see that this is how things work here and that you can’t get ahead without working 12 hours a day. And nobody stops to think.

It doesn’t have to be this way.

That’s why I struggle when people say you can’t do a startup without working like crazy. If you work like crazy, eventually you go crazy. If you own 40% of the company, fine, you’re the one who went all in. But if you own 0.04%? I don’t expect you to go crazy. We’re in a marathon here, and everyone has to save their breath.

People need to care: about the company, the customers, the people, the product. In a startup especially, I think that’s a must. But you can’t exploit it. And it can’t be that if someone goes on a three-day vacation, everything collapses. If that’s the situation, the company has much bigger problems and it’s an unhealthy work environment. In the long run, I have to solve that.

I’m not fooling myself. A startup is much more stressful and demanding than a big company. In a big company, when balls get dropped, there’s often a support network that catches them (or nobody cares that the ball fell). The challenge is to create an environment where even in a startup, when balls fall (and they will), it isn’t a catastrophe.

Is it possible? I think (and hope) so.

What I do know is that this time I’ll take a step back if I see us starting to slide down that slope, and for that we’ve set up a support network of people who will say “stop” in time.

entry.title: Evaluating startup ideas on two axes
entry.content:
For choosing a workplace, or for when a friend at a bar has “the next unicorn, bro”.

I should be working on my talk for Reversim, so of course I’m procrastinating and writing this instead.

This isn’t a personal story, it’s a framework that helps me evaluate ideas. I should say I didn’t read about it anywhere. It’s just something I slowly built for myself in my head, out of observation and past experience.

Every startup begins with a team that has to come together around an idea (not necessarily in that order). As I’ve said before, I don’t think the idea is that important, and it doesn’t need to be airtight. On the contrary, you need some flexibility, because the idea is going to change a thousand times.

But what do you do when you’re thinking about an idea? At first a lot of ideas come up, each of which could take the company somewhere else. They’ll all look genius at first, and an hour later they’ll look stupid.

To help me evaluate an idea, I put it on a set of axes. The X axis is the size of the market, and the Y axis is the difficulty.

Difficulty of solving the problem can be technological (very specific knowledge), procedural (FDA approvals) or about market penetration (getting people to host strangers in their homes). Difficulty is relative, and what’s hard for one team can be easy for another.

Market size is usually measured as total addressable market (TAM), or as we say in Israel: “how much money is in there?” For example, there are hundreds of millions of mobile users, but none of them spends too much on apps. On the other hand, there aren’t many people working in enterprise security, but everyone knows there’s a sea of money there.

Now let’s map each quadrant. To quote my partner On Freund: “the interesting part is on the diagonals”.

Quadrant 1: hard problem, huge market

These are the classic VC companies. There’s a huge market waiting for a solution, and if the team can solve this hard problem, there’s bonanza potential.

Examples: DoorDash (operations at scale), Stitch Fix (an algorithm for a recommendation engine that works), Intuit (bureaucracy).

  • Pros: if you make it through the difficulty (usually a big “if”), there’s potential for big money.
  • Cons: you need to find someone who’ll believe in you and put money on you, commitment, long cycles.

There’s also a subgroup here: super hard problems in an enormous market. Because of the nature of these problems, there’s an underserved audience just waiting for a solution. The players here are the tech giants, because they have tons of money, talent and influence, and they’re thirsty for more market share.

Examples: robots (Amazon), smart cities (Google), internet in third-world countries (Facebook).

Quadrant 2: hard problem, small market

On paper this quadrant isn’t worth the investment, but companies here are betting on a market that keeps growing. The rationale is that if and when the market gets there, they’ll be first in line with the knowledge and the product.

Examples: Beyond Meat (bet on the vegetarian trend), Twilio (SaaS developers), the first mobile developers.

  • Pros: the thrill of being pioneers, and if you solve it but the market doesn’t get there, potential for a good acquisition.
  • Cons: a big bet (on both the solution and the market), and you really have to time the market (being early isn’t good either).

Quadrant 3: easy problem, small market

Classic bootstrap products. DHH says that to reach a million dollars in annual revenue, all you need is 1,000 users paying you $100 a month. Numbers like that are something you can bring in from the garage. On the other hand, funds will shut the door as soon as they see them.

Examples: Basecamp, and thousands of companies you haven’t heard of because they make great money and save on PR.

  • Pros: no big investment or commitment at the start, you can begin while working, passive income.
  • Cons: finding users is very hard, and the moment you’re onto something, someone will copy the product.

Quadrant 4: easy problem, big market

Supposedly the holy grail. But as my economics lecturer said (I didn’t study economics): if they told me there was $100 on the floor, I wouldn’t believe it, because if there were, someone would have already picked it up.

So I always look strangely at a company that says it’s in this area. It will usually be a crowded market (a red ocean), full of big, veteran companies all competing over fractions of a percent.

Examples: simple mobile apps, drop shipping, the world of advertising.

  • Pros: a fast track to acquisition by one of the companies already in the field.
  • Cons: competition isn’t healthy for a business, certainly not against veterans.

What’s next

Two follow-ups I’d like to write and hope I remember: movement between quadrants, because the market is dynamic and companies keep moving along the axes, and how we used this framework to rule out ideas very early, because we knew up front we wanted to live in quadrant 1.

This has been sitting in my head for a long time and I wanted to put it on paper, because I really think it gives people tools to evaluate ideas and their potential. Whether that’s for choosing a workplace, or for when a friend comes to you at a bar with “the next unicorn, bro”.

entry.title: Phantom features
entry.content:
The cheapest way to find out if anyone actually wants it.

Building a product, or even a feature, is expensive. It takes a lot of time and money, and most of the time your assumption about what users need is wrong. When you’re short on time and money (the definition of a startup?) you have to find a shortcut.

So what do you do?

1. Ask users whether they need it. You can, but it’s usually not enough. Users don’t really know what they want, and they’ll say “yes” because why not, especially if the product is offered for free. Experienced people will tell you the distance between saying “yes, I’d buy it” and pulling out a credit card and paying is the distance between heaven and earth.

2. Build an MVP and test it. You can, but it’s not a hit. First because it takes quite a bit of time and money. And second, when the MVP crashes and doesn’t attract users, you will always start finding excuses, because you’re already invested (“it doesn’t have all the features”, “it needs another explanation screen”, “it needs more design”), and you’ll try to make it work.

3. And my favorite: a phantom feature. I have no idea if that’s the official name. You let the user think there’s really something there, take them through the whole flow, and then say “good to know, we’ll get back to you”. That way you’re actually testing on real users.

What does that look like in practice? Eytan Levit once told a story about doing something like this at Mixtiles. They wanted to test a new product, so they built a real landing page with a purchase page, launched an ad campaign and everything. At the end they told users the product was out of stock (and gave them some compensation). That way they could simply test the product’s economic viability.

entry.title: The "it'll be fine" method
entry.content:
Zero buffers. I’m in a hurry, not stressed.

I want to tell you a bit about my time management system, better known as “it’ll be fine”.

The heart of the method is zero buffers and squeezing every second. For example, if I have a meeting on the other side of the floor, I’ll finish what I’m doing just a minute before and run.

I only schedule meetings back to back, especially these days when we work remotely. I end each meeting exactly on the minute, no matter what, and immediately jump into the next one.

If I have a meeting that’s a half-hour drive away, I’ll start getting ready 35 minutes before and leave exactly half an hour before. If I need to eat, I’ll just take something I can eat while driving.

If I know I have something in 10 minutes, I’ll take on another task or phone call, even if it might take 15 minutes, and I’ll finish it in 10.

Why “it’ll be fine”? Because people keep telling me “you won’t make it”, and I say it’ll be fine, and in the vast majority of cases it really is fine. As for the minority that isn’t, I’m willing to take the hit.

From the outside it looks like I have no planning abilities and everything is chaotic, and it sometimes drives the people around me crazy. But for me there’s a strong rationale.

Time is money. A lot of it. There’s no justification for letting 10 minutes drip through your fingers, so I use every time slot bigger than a minute. Parkinson’s law says an hour’s task will take you 45 minutes or two hours, depending on how much time you give it.

So do I never rest during the day? I also make sure to set aside a fixed amount of time for mindfulness.

This could be read as a permanently stressed schedule. I’m in a hurry, not stressed.

Matan Zinger once said I’m like Tom Sawyer: I throw my hat over and now I have to go get it. Yes, I limit myself on purpose to get the most out of it. If I have a meeting in 45 minutes I’ll go for a run, even though I do 5k in half an hour. I’ll just run faster.
